articles.text: We just want to rise up long enough to ask whether, in spite of senator Edmunds and the vigilance of the reporters, president Cleveland has not committed bigamy. We have a collection of newspaper pictures of Mrs. Cleveland, ranging all the way from Bismarck with his mustache cut off and old Mother Bendor to the Venus de Medici. One picture of the collection resembles another about as much as a maverick resembles a hondoo. We don't want to cause any trouble, but either the president has started a harem in the White House or some newspapers are lying about "their remarkably faithful likeness of the President's bride."
articles.summary: Packard jokes that newspaper portraits of the new Mrs. Cleveland vary so widely the President must have a harem.

articles.text: According to recent telegrams, the average reporter's enterprise is only exceeded by the capaciousness of a car platform. We read in the Pioneer Press that "the President thought he had outwitted the reporters in leaving the White House grounds by an almost unused gate to talk a special train for Deer Park, but a Pioneer Press reporter was watching every move the bridal couple made and on his trusty bicycle followed the carriage to the train, which steamed out at 10:55 with a Pioneer Press reporter on the hind platform." Here we thought, is a reporter that will make his mark in the world. Sure enough either he or another one did for the New York World contained exactly the same article, except that in this case it was a World, instead of a Pioneer Press reporter. Here then, are the two rustlers for news who will in time occupy the top notches of journalism. Someway we began to doubt the reporter's veracity when we found that a St Paul Globe repersentative also had a reserved seat on the hind platform. We had scarcely recovered from our surprise when we found that an Inter Ocean reporter was also on the list and the hind platform. By this time the platform must have been rather crowded but a Minneapolis Tribune reporter edged his way on, only to be elbowed by a news friend from the Cincinnati Enquirer. This must have shoved some of them up on the brake wheel but they had to make room for representatives from the Boston Herld, the New York Times, the Indianapolis Journal and the Detroit Free Press. After reading these veracious accounts of the news gathers, we came to the conclusion that either that back platform had a crowding capacity equal to a Chicago street-car or that the reporters were lying. The latter proved true for the special correspondent of the BAD LANDS COW BOY rode on the front platform all the way from Washington to Deer Park and has sent us affidavits that he was the only occupant of that airy perch and that not even a tramp decorated the back platform with his presence.
articles.summary: Packard lampoons the many newspapers that each claimed their reporter rode the hind platform of President Cleveland's honeymoon train to Deer Park.

articles.text: If Mose. Ryder doesn't take care, he will bring a case against himself for malicious maiming. We heard him try to get a man to ride his broncho on a bet of $50 that he couldn't ride him four rods. As we publish no obituary notice this week, the fact speaks for itself that the bet was not taken.

articles.text: The round-up was at the 777 camp Tuesday night, making fast and satisfactory progress. The boys think they will finish by the 15th. Both riders and horses are better than those of any previous round-up here, everything has so far worked to perfection and the general verdict is that this is, as it should be, the best round-up the Bad Lands have yet had.
articles.summary: The round-up reached the 777 camp Tuesday night and was expected to finish by the 15th.

articles.text: We have received several requests for the publication of the official list of the calves branded on the round-up. We find that this is impossible, as each man keeps a count on his own calves and no general list is kept. There is also quite a rivalry among the cow-men as to who shall brand the greatest number of calves; the per cent. not being brought forward as it should be. This fact adds to the difficulty of getting a correct list, as a man hates to say that he only branded two hundred calves while his neighbor has branded five hundred, although the former's per cent. may be much higher than the latter's. We can only say in reference to the general calf crop of the Bad Lands, that it seems to be the universal opinion of the boys on the round-up, that the spring and fall round-ups will show a considerably larger per cent. of calves than we have yet had. The present round-up shows a slight increase over the average, while the prospects are that the showings of the fall round-up will be a decided improvement.
articles.summary: No official list of calves branded on the round-up is kept; the Bad Lands calf crop is reported slightly above average.

articles.text: The total drive from Texas this year has been carefully computed by some of our southern exchanges at 171,000. Of these, the Hashknife company is only credited with 21,000, whereas they now have 36,000 on the trail, for their Little Missouri and Box Elder ranges. According to report, Driskill, Blocker & Davis have 35,000 on the trail; E. S. Newman has 5,000; Mabry & Pryor, 3,000 and Reynolds Bros., 10,000.
articles.summary: The Texas drive is put at 171,000 head; the Hashknife company has 36,000 on the trail for its Little Missouri and Box Elder ranges.

articles.text: Last week when the round-up was at Pierre Wibaux' ranch on Beaver creek, Bronson Rumsey offered five dollars to the cowboy who roped and tied down a steer in the shortest time. Some quick work was done, the prize being taken by Henry Williams who works for Gregor Lang. Time 2:38. Link Gates was second but had bad luck, his rope breaking or he would have rustled Henry, who is one of the best ropers that ever came to the country.
articles.summary: At the round-up at Pierre Wibaux's ranch, Henry Williams (of Gregor Lang's outfit) won Bronson Rumsey's $5 steer-roping prize in 2:38.

articles.text: Opinions as to whether the rain of Monday will start the grass to growing again, are divided. The majority think that the feed will be materially increased, but that it will make a person rustle hard to find hay. Some go so far as to say that there will be no further growth of grass while others think that it is scarcely hurt at all. In Colorado, last year, the ranges had all turned brown by June 20, but rains started the grass again in good shape. We hope to see more rainy weather very soon and as the grass is now manifestly getting a fresh start, all scarcity of feed may be avoided.
articles.summary: Opinion is divided on whether Monday's rain will revive the range grass.

articles.text: The question is being earnestly discussed as to whether it would not be better for the cattle-raisers of the west to erect shambles and do their own butchering, sending dressed beef to market instead of live beef. It was once thought necessary to send all beef on foot to the point where it was to be consumed and have it butchered there. This was before the days of refrigerator store-houses. Already the practice once thought necessary is partially superceded. Dressed beef is shipped from Australia to England, and from this country to our English cousins. Western beef is sent to the eastern states for consumption, and just now Chicago dressed beef is creating considerable excitement in the great cities of the east and southeast, where it comes in competition with that slaughtered by the local butchers. Those who favor the adoption of this method make the following claims: 1. The saving of an untold amount of suffering; 2. It gives healthier meat to consumers; 3. It gives cheaper meat; 4. It gives tenderer meat; 5. It gives better meat in every respect; 6. It gives better prices to the producer; 7. Both the producer and the consumer have the right to the benefits of the age; 8. Hence, no man, or small set of men, have any right to intervene; 9. It is against public policy for common carriers to be so controlled as to sacrifice the public good for the few.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint from the National Live Stock Journal arguing for western dressed-beef slaughtering over shipping live cattle.

articles.headline: The Flocks of the United States.
articles.text:
The Department of Agricultural in a recent report gives the average valuation of sheep per head in several eastern and western states and territories as follows: New Jersey, $3.75; Rhode Island, $3.75; Vermont $2.68; New York, $3.06; Maryland, $3.08; Ohio, $2.00; Texas, $1,70; New Mexico, $1.60.

From the same report it appears that over three-fourths of the sheep in the United States are owned in the following States and Territories; the numbering each being over 1,000,000, disturbuted as follows: Texas, 6,802,615; California, 6,069,698; Ohio, 4,753,034; New Mexico, 4,323,755; Oregon, 2,469,551; Michigan, 2,269,607; New York, 1,595,825; Missouri 1,285,078; Wisconsin, 1,218,800; Kansas, 1,190,163; Pennsylvania, 1,189,481; Colorado, 1,126,647; Indiana, 1,088,157; Illinois, 1,005,653. In these states the average valuation is $1.88 per head, it being the lowest as a rule, where the largest numbers are, Ohio and Michigan being the only states owing over 2,000,000 that show a valuation above $2.00. The states and territories not above enumerated in which about one-fourth are owned showed an average valuation of $2.00. The grand total of the flocks of the United States is, in round numbers, 50,000,000,000, vauled at $95,000,000.—[Journal of Agriculture.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Journal of Agriculture on U.S. sheep numbers and valuations by state.

articles.headline: The Daily Journey of the Horse.
articles.text: According to Hon. John E. Russell, secretary of the Massachusetts board of agriculture, the regular daily journey of the horse should not exceed twelve or thirteen miles. This is as great a distance, he thinks, as can be economically alloted a horse as a day's journey for every day in the week. If he has a longer daily journey, he must have a day or two off each week. This day's work of the travelling horse is based on the experience of stage and car companies. For the stage, where most speed is required, ten miles have been found the limits of an economical day's journey. But a great deal depends on the speed. Give the horse plenty of time and he can do a longer daily journey than he can if he is urged beyond an easy gait. In emergencies, a good horse can do fifty or sixty miles in a day. Seventy-five and eighty miles have been driven. But such long, fast journeys are very trying to the [illegible] and he needs to be managed with great care and judgment to prevent harm from such violent, continued exertion. Such driving cannot be repeated often with safety. The regular day's journey should be lengthened or shortened according to the condition and character of the road and the weight of the load. Then there is a difference in individuals, and what one horse does with ease, may be very hard for another. Feed and care are also factors in the problem not to be overlooked.—[Hoof and Horn.
articles.summary: Reprint from Hoof and Horn on how far a horse should travel each day.

articles.headline: Broncho Bill, from Pizen Spider.
articles.text:
BY WILL VISSCHER.

Well yes, I'm fum Wyoming—
Ain't 'shameed to say so, nuther—
An' I'd ruther be fum that place
En almos' any other.

The mountains is the highest
An we've got the broadest plains;
We irrigate the valleys—
Don't bother atter rains.

Thar's a world of gold and silver,
An' soda 'oil an' coal,
An' cattle on a thousan' hills
Ez fat ez they kin roll.

The sun shines thar the brightest,
An' stays the hull year 'round
An' the climate is the healthiest,
That ever has been found.

The women vote at 'lections,
Ar' wise about it too,
An' they've got a better right to vote
En any dude like you.

I'm a statin' that a woman
Ez is had a half er chance
Allers makes as good a citizen
Ez camps about the ranch.

An' when I make a statement,
An' know it to be squar',
'Tain't safe to go to doubtin' it,
Out here er anywhar.

We've got the broadest set er men
Upon the bloomin' earth,
An' manhood's what we measure by,
An' not the'r blood an' birth.

Thar's room fur 'bout er million—
Er some the rise er that—
An' room enough to all git rich,
An' healthy, strong an' fat.

But they'd orter be the best thar is,
Fur littleness don't pan
In the gorjus territory
That's adjacent to Shyann.
—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted dialect poem by Will Visscher praising Wyoming.

articles.text:
A man afflicted with deafness took a prescription to a druggist, who filled it with care and in the latest style. The deaf man asked the price, when the following talk occured:

Druggist (leaning on the counter and smiling in a won't-you-pay up sort of a manner)—"The price is seventy-five cents."

Deaf Customer—"Five cents? Here it is."

Druggist (in a louder voice)—"Seventy-five cents, please."

Deaf Customer—"Well, there's your five cents."

Druggist (in a very loud voice and very firm manner)—"I said seventy-five cents."

Deaf Customer (getting angry)—"Well, what more do you want? I just gave you five cents."

Druggist (sotto voice)—"Well, go to thunder with your medicine; I made three cents, anyway."—[Drug Record.
articles.summary: Reprinted joke from the Drug Record about a deaf customer and a druggist.

articles.text: In Judge Seaton's court last Saturday, Mr. A. 1. Stiff was brought up under the vagrant act. A jury of our most reputable citizens was impanelled after considerable difficulty, juror Garver firmly refusing to serve or render a verdict until his fees, amounting to two bits, had finally compromised on a pipeful of tobacco, donated by Judge Seaton. Prosecuting attorney Gordon presented the case for the Territory and handled the subject ably. He ransacked ancient and modern history to furnish examples of the worthlessness of mankind and for pure, unadulterated, cussed uselessness, pronounced the prisoner at the bar "facile princeps." (We don't know what that means and disclaim any responsibility for any hidden meaning or dynamite lurking about it-Ed.) Attorney Wadsworth for the defence, acknowledged that "my clint may be a laverick, with no regular grazing gorunds and no brand on him except the stamp of genius, but, gentlemen of the jury, examine him carefully, look at the ear-marks of talent that crop out all over him, take a look at his eyes, unbleared by anything except budge, notice the hidden mine of wealth he would be to our saloon-keepers if his pocket-book were not a personification of emptiness and turn him loose to pick a living from eastern tenderfeet." The attorney's eloquence was here interrupted by juror Gar[ver?], whose pipe had gone out. After relighting this source of inspiration, the jury retired and agreeed on a verdict immediately, but refused to bring it in unless a bottle of lubricant was furnished. Pending a discussion of Ways and Means committee as to how this could be provided, a freight train came in and Mr. A. 1. Stiff went sailing out of town on a break beam.
articles.summary: Comic account of a vagrancy trial in Judge Seaton's court; the defendant "A. 1. Stiff" left town on a freight train before the verdict.

articles.text: Referring to the Cow Boy account of the shovel-nosed fish caught recently here by Billy Reach, the Billings Gazette says: "The fish caught by Billy was undoubtedly the shovel-nosed sturgeon, which was, in the early days of Miles City and Billings, a staple article of diet. The Gazette drew attention to the wonderful amount of nutrition in these fish some time ago. They swell, upon mastication, so much that two small bites make a good square meal for a hungry man. They are probably identical with the two small fish that feasted a multitude in Scriptural days."
articles.summary: The Billings Gazette identifies Billy Reach's shovel-nosed fish as a shovel-nosed sturgeon.

articles.text:
[First publication May 6.]

TER. OF DAKOTA, COUNTY OF MORTON, To which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes. SS.

Notice is hereby given that by virtue of a judgment and decree in foreclosure, rendered and given by the District Court of the sixth judicial district, in and for the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, and filed in the office of said court, on the 23rd. day of April, A. D. 1886, in an action wherein the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company is plaintiff and John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer are defendants, in favor of said plaintiff, and against said defendant, for the sum of One thousand three hundred and twenty-seven dollars and fifty-three cents ($1,327.53,) the principal and interest secured by a certain mortgage, given by John Kiefer and Mary J Kiefer, his wife, to the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, together with interest thereon from April 10th., A. D. 1886, the date of said decree and also the cost of said plaintiff, taxed at the sum of ninety-one dollars and thirty-five cents, ($91.35,) which judgment and decree directed the sale by me of the real estate hereinafter described, to satisfy the amount of said judgment, with interest thereon, and costs and expenses of said sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy, and by virtue of a writ issued out of the office of the Clerk of said court, in and for said county of Morton, to which county, Billings county is attached for judicial purposes, and under the seal of said court, directing me to sell said real property, pursuant to said judgment and decree,

I, George W. Harmon, Sheriff of said Morton county and the person appointed by said court to make said sale, will sell the hereinafter described real estate to the highest bidder, for cash, at public auction, at the front door of the Court House in the city of Mandan, in the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, on the 17th day of June, A. D. 1886, at two o'clock P. M., of that day, to satisfy said judgment, interest and costs, and the costs and expenses of such sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy.

The premises to be sold as aforesaid, pursuant to said judgment and decree, and to said writ, and to [this?] notice, are described in said judgment, decree and writ, as follows, to-wit:

All those tracts or parcels of land lying and being in the County of Billings, and Territory of Dakota, described as follows:

Lots number Thirteen (13) and Fourteen (14) in Block number nine (9,) as laid down and designated on the plat of the town of Medora, Billings county, D. T., as the same is recorded in the office of Register of Deeds of Morton county, D. T., to which County Billings county, which is unorganized, is attached for judicial purposes.

Dated at Mandan, Dakota. April 29, A. D., 1886.
George W. Harmon, Sheriff, Morton County, Dakota.
Edward S. Allen, Plaintiff's Att'y.

STATE OF PENNSYLVANIA, Washington County, ss.
On this 28th. day of April, A. D. 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and State, personally appeared Julius LeMoyue and in his own name and for himself and in the name of his constituent John A. Wills, and in due form of law, acknowledged the within instrument of writing to be his act and deed and the act and deed of his constituent, the said John A. Wills, to the end that the same be recorded as such.
Witness my hand and notarial seal, the day and year aforesaid.
T. F. Birch, Notary Public. [Notarial Seal.]

STATE OF PENNSYLVANIA, County of Allegheny. ss.
On this 30th. day of April, A. D., 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and State, personally aapeared W. A. Nicholson, Edward E. Phelps, Charles H. Bradley, Pennock Hart, William Wade, Trustee, M. Fundenberg, Joseph U. Rose, M. C. Byrnes, Thomas H. Hartley, Webster Gray, Frak Shanley, Howard Hartley, Trustee and S. I. Boggs and in due form of law acknowledged the within instrument of writing to be their act and deed, to the end that the same be recorded as such.
Witness my hand and notarial seal the day and year above written.
Henry C. Lyon, Notary Public. [Notarial Seal.]

TERRITORY OF DAKOTA, County of Morton. ss.
On this 4th. day of May, A. D., 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and Territory, personally appeared H. T. Hallock, to me personally known to be the same person described in and who executed the foregoing instrument and acknowledged to me that he executed the same for the uses and purposes therein expressed.
[Notarial Seal.] Elbridge C. Cooke, Notary Public, Dakota Ter.
